tiers.name: Foundations
tiers.blurb: Common shapes, no expanded octets, no formal-charge tug-of-war. Get the rhythm of the five stages here.

molecules.name: Methane
molecules.polarityReason: Four identical C-H bonds at 109.5 degrees in a perfectly tetrahedral arrangement. The four small bond dipoles point at the corners of a tetrahedron and the vector sum is zero, so the molecule has no net dipole.
molecules.commonTrap: Students see four hydrogens and assume CH4 must be polar because C and H differ in electronegativity. The bonds are slightly polar, but the tetrahedral symmetry cancels them perfectly. Polarity always needs polar bonds AND asymmetric geometry.

molecules.name: Ammonia
molecules.polarityReason: Three N-H bonds are polar (N is more electronegative than H) and the lone pair on nitrogen breaks the symmetry. The three bond dipoles point down at N and the lone pair adds electron density on top, giving a strong net dipole.
molecules.commonTrap: Forgetting the lone pair when picking molecular geometry. Students see three bonds and call ammonia trigonal planar at 120 degrees. The fourth electron group (the lone pair) makes the electron geometry tetrahedral and pushes the H atoms down into a pyramid at 107 degrees.

molecules.name: Water
molecules.polarityReason: Two strongly polar O-H bonds plus a bent geometry from two lone pairs on oxygen. The bond dipoles do not point opposite each other, so they add into a large net dipole pointing from the H atoms toward the oxygen.
molecules.commonTrap: Calling the molecular geometry tetrahedral because there are four electron groups. Molecular geometry names atoms only. With two bonds and two lone pairs, oxygen is sp3 (tetrahedral electron geometry) but the molecular shape is bent.

molecules.name: Carbon dioxide
molecules.polarityReason: Both C=O bonds are strongly polar but they point in exactly opposite directions along a 180-degree line. Two equal vectors at 180 degrees sum to zero, so CO2 is nonpolar despite having very polar bonds.
molecules.commonTrap: Drawing two single bonds and stopping. Carbon needs an octet, and with only single bonds it has just four electrons. The fix is two double bonds (O=C=O), which is also why the molecule is linear with sp hybridization.

molecules.name: Beryllium chloride
molecules.polarityReason: Beryllium is an octet exception with only two bonding pairs and no lone pairs, so the two Be-Cl bonds sit at 180 degrees. The bond dipoles cancel exactly, leaving the molecule nonpolar.
molecules.commonTrap: Forcing an octet on beryllium. Be is happy with only four electrons (two single bonds). Trying to add lone pairs to Be or use double bonds invents formal charges that do not need to exist.

molecules.name: Boron trifluoride
molecules.polarityReason: Boron is also an octet exception with only six electrons. Three identical B-F bonds sit at 120 degrees in a flat plane. Three equal vectors evenly spaced sum to zero, so the molecule is nonpolar.
molecules.commonTrap: Adding a B=F double bond to give boron an octet. The lower-energy structure leaves boron at six electrons and keeps formal charges at zero. Boron and beryllium are the classic octet exceptions on the DAT.

tiers.name: Build
tiers.blurb: Formal charges, resonance, and the first expanded octets. This is where the rhythm gets tested.

molecules.name: Nitrate
molecules.polarityReason: Three equivalent N-O bonds (averaged by resonance) at 120 degrees in a flat plane. The bond dipoles cancel by symmetry. Note: this asks about the neutral 'shape polarity' of the ion; the ion itself carries a -1 charge.
molecules.commonTrap: Forgetting to add an electron for the negative charge. Total valence is 5 + 18 + 1 = 24, not 23. Then students often draw three single bonds and miss that one N=O double bond is required to give nitrogen an octet without expanded valence (period 2 only has s and p orbitals).

molecules.name: Sulfur dioxide
molecules.polarityReason: Two polar S-O bonds plus a lone pair on sulfur. The bent geometry means the bond dipoles do not cancel, and the lone pair contributes its own electron density, giving SO2 a clear net dipole.
molecules.commonTrap: Treating SO2 like CO2 because both are AX2. SO2 has a lone pair on the central atom, which makes it bent (not linear) and polar (not nonpolar). The fingerprint is the steric number: SO2 is steric 3, CO2 is steric 2.

molecules.name: Sulfur trioxide
molecules.polarityReason: Three equivalent S-O bonds (one double bond delocalized by resonance) sit at 120 degrees in a flat plane. The three bond dipoles are equal in magnitude and 120 degrees apart, so the vector sum is zero.
molecules.commonTrap: Confusing SO3 with SO2. Same atoms, very different molecule. SO3 has no lone pair on sulfur, so it is trigonal planar and nonpolar. SO2 has a lone pair on sulfur, so it is bent and polar.

molecules.name: Ammonium
molecules.polarityReason: Four identical N-H bonds at 109.5 degrees in a tetrahedral arrangement. The bond dipoles cancel by symmetry, so the ion has no net molecular dipole. The +1 ionic charge is a separate property from molecular polarity.
molecules.commonTrap: Forgetting to subtract an electron for the positive charge. Total valence is 5 + 4 - 1 = 8, not 9. Students who draw NH4+ with a lone pair on nitrogen end up with a formal charge of -1 on N rather than +1.

molecules.name: Phosphorus pentachloride
molecules.polarityReason: Five identical P-Cl bonds in a trigonal bipyramidal arrangement. The two axial dipoles cancel each other along the vertical axis, and the three equatorial dipoles cancel each other in the horizontal plane. Net dipole is zero.
molecules.commonTrap: Calling PCl5 an octet violation as if that disqualifies it. Period 3 elements (P, S, Cl) can use d-orbitals to expand past eight electrons. PCl5 has ten electrons around phosphorus, and that is allowed.

molecules.name: Sulfur hexafluoride
molecules.polarityReason: Six identical S-F bonds at 90 degrees to each other in an octahedral arrangement. Every bond has an exact partner on the opposite side, so each pair of dipoles cancels and the molecule has zero net dipole despite very polar S-F bonds.
molecules.commonTrap: Assuming SF6 must be polar because S-F is one of the most polar bonds in the bank. The geometry is the deciding factor: octahedral with six identical terminal atoms is one of the canonical symmetric shapes, so all the polar bonds cancel.

tiers.name: Mastery
tiers.blurb: Five-group and six-group lone-pair placement. This is what separates a 25 from a 22 on DAT GC.

molecules.name: Sulfur tetrafluoride
molecules.polarityReason: Four polar S-F bonds plus one lone pair in the equatorial plane. The lone pair breaks the symmetry of the trigonal bipyramid, so the bond dipoles no longer cancel. The molecule has a net dipole pointing away from the lone pair.
molecules.commonTrap: Putting the lone pair in an axial position. In a trigonal bipyramid, lone pairs always go equatorial because the equatorial position has two 90-degree neighbors and two 120-degree neighbors instead of three 90-degree neighbors. Equatorial lone pair gives see-saw, not trigonal pyramidal.

molecules.name: Bromine trifluoride
molecules.polarityReason: Three polar Br-F bonds plus two lone pairs on bromine, both equatorial. The two axial fluorines cancel each other, but the third equatorial fluorine has no partner. The net dipole points along the equatorial Br-F bond.
molecules.commonTrap: Calling BrF3 trigonal planar at 120 degrees because there are three bonds. The two equatorial lone pairs squeeze the three F atoms into a T-shape: two axial and one equatorial, with bond angles slightly less than 90 degrees.

molecules.name: Xenon difluoride
molecules.polarityReason: Three lone pairs sit in the equatorial plane and the two fluorines occupy the axial positions, 180 degrees apart. The two Xe-F dipoles point in exactly opposite directions and cancel, so the molecule is nonpolar.
molecules.commonTrap: Calling XeF2 bent like H2O because both have only two bonded atoms. XeF2 has five electron groups (three lone pairs, two bonds), and the lone pairs all go equatorial. That forces the F atoms to the axial positions, giving a linear molecular shape, not bent.

molecules.name: Xenon tetrafluoride
molecules.polarityReason: Two lone pairs sit on opposite sides of the octahedron (180 degrees apart). The four fluorines fall into a flat square at 90 degrees. Each Xe-F dipole has an equal partner directly across the square, so all dipoles cancel and the molecule is nonpolar.
molecules.commonTrap: Putting the two lone pairs at adjacent (90-degree) positions on the octahedron, which would give a see-saw or distorted shape. Lone pairs in an octahedron always go trans (180 degrees apart) to minimize lone-pair to lone-pair repulsion. That trans placement is what makes XeF4 square planar and nonpolar.

molecules.name: Chlorine trifluoride
molecules.polarityReason: Three polar Cl-F bonds with two equatorial lone pairs on chlorine. The two axial F atoms cancel each other, but the equatorial F has no partner across from it. The net dipole points along the equatorial Cl-F bond.
molecules.commonTrap: Treating ClF3 as if the second lone pair could go axial. In a trigonal bipyramid, both lone pairs go equatorial because each equatorial slot has fewer 90-degree neighbors than an axial slot. Two equatorial lone pairs plus one equatorial F gives the T-shape with two axial F atoms.

molecules.name: Iodine pentafluoride
molecules.polarityReason: Five polar I-F bonds plus one lone pair on iodine. The lone pair takes one of the six octahedral positions and pushes the iodine slightly out of the square-base plane. The four square-base dipoles cancel each other, but the apical I-F has no partner, leaving a clear net dipole.
molecules.commonTrap: Calling IF5 trigonal bipyramidal because there are five bonded F atoms. With one lone pair, the steric number is six, so the electron geometry is octahedral. The lone pair sits opposite the apical fluorine, giving square pyramidal geometry. AX5E is square pyramidal, never trigonal bipyramidal.
